overview.body:
**Vajrapāṇi** (*vajrapani*) ​— Thunderbolt ‌Holder, Protection · ‌The Vajra-Bearer, ​Lord of Secret ​Power — ​is the bodhisattva ​of power: the ​vajra-wielding guardian ‌who began as ​the Buddha's ​personal protector in ‌the earliest ​texts and grew ‌into the ​lord of the ‌tantric mysteries, ​keeper of the ​thunderbolt and ​of every secret ​the tradition ​ever whispered.[^1]

The ‌name is a ​bahuvrīhi: *vajra-pāṇi*, ‌‘in whose hand ​is the ‌vajra’ — the ​thunderbolt-sceptre that ‌is at once ​Indra's weapon, ‌the diamond of ​unbreakable truth, ​and the ritual ‌implement of ‌the Vajrayāna. The ‌word is ​older than Buddhism: ​Monier-Williams records *vajrapāṇi* ‌as an ​epithet of Indra ​in the ‌Brāhmaṇas and the ​Mahābhārata, the ​storm-god ‘with the ‌bolt in ​hand’.[^2] Buddhism took ‌the title ​and made it ​a biography: ​the Pāli canon ​knows Vajirapāṇi ‌the yakṣa who ‌guards the Buddha's ​debates; Gandhāran ‌art gives him ​Herakles' own ​body beside the ‌master; the ‌Mahāyāna enthrones him ‌with [[manjushri|Mañjuśrī]] ‌and Avalokiteśvara as ​one of ‌the three great ​protectors — ​wisdom, power, and ​compassion; and ‌the tantras make ​him Guhyakādhipati, Lord ​of the ​Secret Ones, the ‌compiler and ​keeper of the ​esoteric canon.

​PuniCodex restores the ‌name as ​**Vajrapāṇi** and serves ‌its temple ​at [vajrapāṇi.com](https://xn--vajrapi-x3a0658d.com). The ‌restoration keeps ​the long ā ‌and the ‌retroflex ṇ; the ​plain ASCII *vajrapani* ​is a ​modern convenience of ​the early ‌domain-name system, not ‌an attested ​ancient spelling.[^2]

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (New York: Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Vajrapāṇi’.
Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. vajrapāṇi, vajra, pāṇi.

the-name.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in Sanskrit as ‌**वज्रपाणि** (IAST *vajrapāṇi*; ​Pāli *Vajirapāṇi*): ​a bahuvrīhi compound ​of *vajra*, ​‘thunderbolt, diamond’, and ​*pāṇi*, ‘hand’ ‌— ‘the vajra-handed ​one’.[^1] The title ​is inherited ‌from Vedic religion, ​where it ‌belongs to Indra, ​wielder of ‌the bolt that ​splits the dragon ​Vṛtra; the ​Brāhmaṇas and the ​Mahābhārata use ​*vajrapāṇi* as Indra's ‌standing epithet.[^2] Buddhism's ​adoption is ‌a conscious transfer ​of power: ‌the thunderbolt passes ​from the ‌storm-god to the ​Buddha's own protector, ‌and the ​weapon is re-read ​as the ‌diamond of the ‌indestructible teaching.

‌The ASCII form ​*vajrapani* survives only ​because the ‌early domain-name system ​could not ​carry diacritics; it ‌is a technological ​compromise, not ​an ancient spelling. ‌The Unicode ​restoration **Vajrapāṇi** recovers ‌the long ​ā of *pāṇi* ​and the retroflex ​ṇ directly ​in the address ‌bar. Because ‌the restoration preserves ​vowel length and ‌a distinctive ​letter the ASCII ​form loses, ‌the name is ‌classified Tier ‌1.

The letter-by-letter ‌transformation runs:

- ​**v** → ‌**V** — Same, ​capitalized
- ​**a** → **a** ​— Same
‌- **j** → ​**j** — Same
​- **r** ​→ **r** — ‌Same
- ​**a** → **a** ​— Same
- ​**p** → ‌**p** — Same
​- **a** ‌→ **ā** — ​Long vowel ‌ā
- **n** ​→ **ṇ** — ‌Retroflex ṇ
‌- **i** → ​**i** — ​Same

The project ​holds the ​domain **vajrapāṇi.com** (xn--vajrapi-x3a0658d.com) ‌as the canonical ‌home of ​this name.

sources.citation: Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. vajrapāṇi.
Edgerton, Franklin, Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit Grammar and Dictionary, vol. 2 (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1953), s.v. Vajrapāṇi.

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name is ​**/ʋə.dʑrə.ˈpaː.ɳi/** ​— Sanskrit ​Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme ​by phoneme:

​- ‌**Va-** — ​Labial approximant ​[ʋ] (between ‌English ​v and ‌w) with ​short [ə]
‌- ​**-jra-** — ​Voiced palatal ​stop [dʑ] ​with ​trilled [r] ‌and short ​[ə]: the ‌thunderbolt, ​*vajra*
- ‌**-pā-** — ​Voiceless bilabial ‌[p] ​with long ‌[aː]; the ​stressed syllable, ​‘hand’
‌- **-ṇi** ‌— Retroflex ‌nasal [ɳ] ​with ​short [i], ‌tongue curled ​back

For ​the ‌modern speaker, ​the closest ​approximation is: ‌‘vuj-ruh-PAH-nih’ ​— stress ‌the pā, ​curl the ​final ​n.

Kindred ​and historical ‌forms of ‌the ​name:

- ‌**Sanskrit** — ​वज्रपाणि (vajrapāṇi), ​‘vajra-in-hand’
‌- **Pāli** ‌— Vajirapāṇi, ‌the yakṣa ‌guardian ​of the ‌canon
- ​**Tibetan** — ​Phyag ​na rdo ‌rje (Chana ​Dorjé), ‘the ​Vajra ​in the ‌Hand’
- ​**Japanese** — ​Shūkongōjin ​/ Kongōshu, ‌the vajra-bearing ​guardians (the ‌Niō ​of the ‌temple gates)

​Vajrapāṇi is ‌Tier ‌1 because ​the long ​ā and ​the ​retroflex ṇ ‌are both ‌lost in ​ASCII.

sources.citation: Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. vajrapāṇi.

domains.body:
**Vajrapāṇi** ​is the ‌bodhisattva ‌of śakti ​— ​power, force, ​might ​— the ​strong arm ‌of ​the Buddhist ​pantheon.[^1]

‌### The ​Buddha's ‌Protector

From ​the ‌Pāli canon ​onward ​he is ​the ​guardian at ​the ‌teacher's shoulder: ​the power ‌that ​enforces the ‌space ​in which ‌teaching ​can happen.

‌### ​Lord of ​the ‌Secret Ones

‌As ‌Guhyakādhipati he ​is ​master of ‌the guhyakas, ​the ​secret beings, ‌and ​keeper of ​the ‌tantric canon ​— ‌the esoteric ​tradition's ​patron and ​gatekeeper.[^2]

​### The ‌Vajra Itself

‌He ​embodies the ‌implement ​he carries: ​the ‌diamond that ‌breaks ‌all things ‌and ​is broken ‌by ​none — ​the ​figure of ‌an indestructible ​mind.

​### One ​of ‌the Three ​Protectors

​With [[manjushri|Mañjuśrī]] ​(wisdom) ‌and Avalokiteśvara ​(compassion) ‌he completes ​the ‌triad of ​the ‌Lords of ‌the Three ​Families: ​the bodhisattva's ​full ​equipment of ‌insight, ‌power, and ​love.

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Vajrapāṇi’.
Getty, Alice, The Gods of Northern Buddhism (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1914).

symbols.body:
The ​iconography of ‌Vajrapāṇi is ‌a ​single object ​and its ​force:[^1]

​- **The ​vajra** — ‌The ​thunderbolt-sceptre, held ​aloft ‌or at ​the hip: ‌symmetrical ​prongs closed ‌around a ​central ​axis, Indra's ​weapon become ​the ​diamond of ‌unbreakable wisdom
​- ‌**The wrathful ​body** — ‌In ​his fierce ‌forms ​(Caṇḍa-Vajrapāṇi, Nīlāmbaradhara): ‌dark blue, ​fanged, ​garlanded with ‌serpents, standing ‌in ‌the warrior's ​pose — ​protection ‌wears a ​frightening face
​- ‌**The serpents** ​— His ​ornaments ‌are nāgas, ​the ‌serpent spirits ​he subdued ​and ​now wears ​as trophies
‌- ‌**The club-bearing ​attendant** — ‌In ​Gandhāran art ​he stands ‌beside ‌the Buddha ‌in the ‌very ​body of ‌Herakles, ​club or ​vajra in ​hand: ‌the earliest ​Buddhist bodhisattva ​image, ​and the ‌clearest Greco-Buddhist ​fusion ​on record[^2]
​- **The ‌wrestler's ​build** — ‌His physique ​is ‌the strongman's: ​the ‌temple-guardian body ‌that Japan ​would ​split into ​the two ​Niō ‌kings at ‌every monastery ​gate

sources.citation: Getty, Alice, The Gods of Northern Buddhism (Clarendon Press, 1914).
Foucher, Alfred, L'art gréco-bouddhique du Gandhāra (Paris: Ernest Leroux, 1905–22), on the Herakles-Vajrapāṇi type.

mythology.body:
Vajrapāṇi's mythology ​is the transformation ‌of a bodyguard ‌into a cosmic ​officer, traceable stage ​by stage through the ​texts.[^1]

### The ​Enforcer of the ​Canon (Pāli Nikāyas)

‌In the Ambaṭṭha ​Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya ​3), when the ‌young brahmin Ambaṭṭha ​thrice refuses the ‌Buddha's question, the ​yakṣa Vajirapāṇi appears overhead ‌with an iron ​bolt blazing, ready ​to split the ​stubborn man's head ​into seven pieces; ​Ambaṭṭha answers. The ‌Pāli commentaries identify ​the vajra-bearer with ‌Sakka (Indra) himself — ​the old thunderer ‌still serving the ​new dispensation, enforcing ‌not doctrine but ​honesty in dialogue.[^2]

‌### The Attendant ​of Gandhāra

In ​the art of ‌Gandhāra (1st–3rd c. ‌CE), Vajrapāṇi becomes the ‌Buddha's constant companion ​in stone: a ​muscular attendant at ‌the master's shoulder, ​rendered with the ​physique, club, and ‌sometimes the lion-skin ​of Herakles — ​the clearest case ‌of a Greek god's ​body entering the ‌Buddhist pantheon, carrying ​the hero's strength ​into the teacher's ​service.[^3]

### The ​Third Protector (Mahāyāna)

‌The Mahāyāna raised ‌him to the ​triad of great ‌bodhisattvas: [[manjushri|Mañjuśrī]] of wisdom, ​Avalokiteśvara of compassion, ​Vajrapāṇi of power ‌— the Lords ‌of the Three ‌Families (Tibetan *rigs ‌gsum mgon po*), ​a grouping so ‌stable it structures ​iconography from Nepal ​to Mongolia.[^1]

### Lord ​of the Mysteries ‌(Tantra)

The esoteric ​tradition made him ​the keeper of ​its whole canon: ‌as Guhyakādhipati, ‘Lord ​of the Secret ​Ones’, he is ​the being to whom ‌the Buddha entrusts ​the tantras, the ‌interlocutor of the ​Guhyasamāja cycle, and ‌the compiler who ​preserves the esoteric ‌teaching between revelations. ‌His wrathful forms ​— Caṇḍa-Vajrapāṇi, the ​serpent-garlanded Nīlāmbaradhara — guard ​the threshold of ​every maṇḍala: the ‌mysteries have a ‌doorkeeper, and he ​is it.[^4]

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Vajrapāṇi’.
Dīgha Nikāya 3 (Ambaṭṭha Sutta), trans. Maurice Walshe, The Long Discourses of the Buddha (Boston: Wisdom, 1995), with the commentary.
Foucher, Alfred, L'art gréco-bouddhique du Gandhāra (Ernest Leroux, 1905–22).
Getty, Alice, The Gods of Northern Buddhism (Clarendon Press, 1914).

syncretism.body:
Vajrapāṇi ​is one ‌of the ‌great cross-cultural ​transfers in ​religious ​history. His ​title is ​Indra's own ‌— ​the Vedic ​thunderer's epithet ‌inherited and ​re-employed — ‌and ​his body ‌in the ​earliest Buddhist ​art is ​Herakles': ​the Gandhāran ​workshops gave ‌the Buddha ​a ‌Greek hero ​for a ‌bodyguard, and ​the type ‌was ​so successful ‌it travelled ​the whole ​Silk ‌Road.[^1] East ‌Asia then ‌split him ​in two ​at ‌the temple ​gate: the ​Niō kings ‌of Japan ​(Agyō ​with open ‌mouth, Ungyō ​with closed ‌— ​the alpha ​and omega ​of speech) ​are Vajrapāṇi ‌divided ‌into a ​pair, the ‌strongest men ​of the ​pantheon ‌posted at ‌every threshold.[^2]

‌In Tibet ‌he ​is Chana ‌Dorjé, third ​of the ​Three Lords ​and ‌one of ​the most ​invoked protectors ​of ‌the Vajrayāna, ​his dark ​wrathful forms ​flanking every ‌maṇḍala's ​entrance. Kindred ‌figures in ​the PuniCodex ‌index include ​[[manjushri|Mañjuśrī]] ‌(his brother-protector) ‌and [[shiva|Śiva]] ​(the Indic ​tradition's ​other great ​lord of ‌the vajra-club ‌world of ​guardians).

sources.citation: Foucher, Alfred, L'art gréco-bouddhique du Gandhāra (Ernest Leroux, 1905–22).
Getty, Alice, The Gods of Northern Buddhism (Clarendon Press, 1914), on the Niō.

cultural-legacy.body:
Vajrapāṇi's ​most visible ‌legacy ‌stands ​at the ​gates ​of East ​Asian ​Buddhism: ‌the two ​colossal ​Niō ‌guardians — ​the ‌Kongōrikishi — ​whose ‌Nara-period ​masterpieces at ​Tōdai-ji ​(by the ​sculptors ​Unkei ‌and Kaikei, ​1203) ‌are ​among the ‌most ​famous wooden ‌statues ​in ‌the world, ​thunderbolt ​bodies in ‌permanent ‌mid-shout.[^1] ‌Every Japanese ​child ​who ‌has passed ​a ​temple gate ‌has ​met ​him twice.

‌The ​deeper legacy ‌is ​ritual. ​The vajra ​he ​carries became ‌the ‌Vajrayāna's ​very name ‌and ​its ​central implement ‌— ‌the bell-and-bolt ‌pair ‌(vajra ​and ghaṇṭā) ‌of ​every Tibetan ​altar ​— ‌so that ​the ​bodhisattva's ​attribute became ‌a ​whole branch ​of ​Buddhism's ‌identity. As ​Chana ‌Dorjé he ​remains, ‌with ​Avalokiteśvara and ‌Mañjuśrī, ‌one ​of the ​three ​most practised ​protector-deities ‌of ‌the Himalayan ​world.[^2]

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Buddhist Art’, ‘Vajrapāṇi’.
Getty, Alice, The Gods of Northern Buddhism (Clarendon Press, 1914).

archaeology.body:
Vajrapāṇi's ​material record ‌is ‌among the ​oldest of ​any ​bodhisattva's. The ​Gandhāran ​schist reliefs ‌of ​the 1st–3rd ​centuries ‌CE repeatedly ​show the ‌vajra-bearing ​attendant at ‌the ​Buddha's side ​— ​in the ​Miraculous ​Birth, the ‌Great Departure, ​the ‌assault of ​[[mara|Māra]], ‌and the ​parinirvāṇa ‌— rendered, ​as ‌Foucher first ​demonstrated, on ​the ‌model of ‌Herakles: ‌the earliest ​securely ​identifiable bodhisattva ‌figure ​in Buddhist ​art.[^1]

The ‌type ​then diffused ​along ‌the Silk ​Road ‌into the ​Central ​Asian cave ​temples and ​East ‌Asia, where ‌the ​guardian's body ‌became ​the Niō ​pair: ‌the Tōdai-ji ‌gate statues ‌of ‌Unkei and ​Kaikei ‌(1203 CE) ​are ​the supreme ​surviving ‌examples, designated ​National Treasures ​of ​Japan.[^2] In ‌the ​Himalayan world, ​his ​wrathful bronze ‌forms ​— Caṇḍa-Vajrapāṇi ‌and the ​serpent-garlanded ‌protectors — ​fill ‌the temple ‌treasuries ​of Nepal ​and ​Tibet, the ​threshold-keepers of ‌a ‌thousand maṇḍala ​halls.

sources.citation: Foucher, Alfred, L'art gréco-bouddhique du Gandhāra (Ernest Leroux, 1905–22).
Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Buddhist Art’.

meditation.body:
Every ​tradition ‌needs one ‌figure ​who ​is allowed ​to ​be ​strong. Buddhism, ‌which ​distrusts ​force as ‌a ​first ‌principle, still ​kept ‌Vajrapāṇi ​at the ​Buddha's ​shoulder ​— because ​the ‌space ​for gentleness ‌has ​to ‌be defended, ​and ‌honesty, ​in the ‌Ambaṭṭha ​Sutta's ​hard lesson, ‌sometimes ‌needs ‌a blazing ​bolt ​overhead ‌before it ​will ​speak.

‌His secrecy ​is ​the ‌deeper teaching. ​The ‌Lord ​of the ​Secret ​Ones ​does not ‌hide ‌power ​to hoard ‌it; ​he ​holds it ‌until ‌it ‌can be ‌wielded ​without ‌harm. The ​vajra's ​two ​natures are ‌his ​whole ​psychology: the ​thunderbolt ‌that ​breaks everything, ​and ​the ‌diamond that ​nothing ‌breaks. ​He asks ‌of ​anyone ‌who would ‌be ​strong: ​which of ​the ​two ‌are you ‌practising ​today?

sources.citation: Dīgha Nikāya 3 (Ambaṭṭha Sutta), trans. Walshe (1995).

pali-canon.body:
Vajrapāṇi ​is one ‌of ‌the very ​few ​celestial bodhisattvas ​with ​a genuine ​Pāli footprint. ‌The ​**Ambaṭṭha Sutta** ​(DN ‌3) stages ​his ‌most famous ​appearance: ‌when the ​brahmin ​Ambaṭṭha three ​times ​declines the ​Buddha's ‌question about ​his lineage, ‌the ​yakṣa Vajirapāṇi ‌manifests ​above him ‌brandishing ​a blazing ‌iron ​bolt, vowing ​to ‌split his ‌head ‌into seven ​pieces ​— and ‌the young ​man ​finds his ‌voice.[^1] ​The scene ​is ‌repeated in ​kindred ‌discourses and ​glossed ​by the ​commentary, ​which identifies ‌Vajirapāṇi with ‌Sakka, ​king of ‌the ​gods: the ​Vedic ‌Indra's thunderbolt ‌still ‌in service, ‌now ​guarding the ‌Buddha's ​debates rather ​than ​the gods' ‌heaven.

The ​canon ​keeps him ​in ‌this register ​— ​enforcer of ​honest ‌dialogue, guardian ​of ‌the teacher ​— ‌and the ​Mahāyāna's ‌later enthronements ‌all grow ​from ​this seed: ​the ​power that ‌protects ‌the Dharma's ​space.[^2]

sources.citation: Walshe, Maurice, trans., The Long Discourses of the Buddha (Wisdom, 1995): DN 3 (Ambaṭṭha Sutta).
Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Vajrapāṇi’.

mahayana-sutras.body:
In ​the Mahāyāna ‌sūtras ‌Vajrapāṇi rises ​from ​bodyguard to ​officer ​of ​the canon. ‌He ​appears across ​the ‌great collections ​as ‌the protector ​of ‌assemblies and ​the ​subduer of ​the ​nāgas, and ​the ‌Tathāgatācintyaguhyanirdeśa ​— the ‌‘Secrets ​of the ‌Tathāgata’ ​— casts ‌him ​as chief ‌interlocutor ​on the ​mysteries ‌of the ‌Buddha's ‌body, speech, ​and ​mind, ‌a role ​that ​makes him ‌the ​esoteric tradition's ​natural ‌patron.[^1]

The ​tantras ‌complete the ​enthronement: ​as **Guhyakādhipati**, ​Lord ​of the ‌Secret ‌Ones, ​he convenes ‌the ​assemblies of ​the ‌Guhyasamāja cycle ‌and ‌receives the ‌Buddha's ​esoteric teachings ‌into ​his keeping ​— ​the being ‌to ​whom ​the mysteries ​are ‌entrusted until ​the ​time for ​their ‌teaching ripens. ​His ‌wrathful emanations, ​from ‌Caṇḍa-Vajrapāṇi to ​the ‌serpent-garlanded Nīlāmbaradhara, ‌guard ​the ​gates of ​the ​maṇḍala and ‌the ‌meditation manuals ​alike.[^2]

sources.citation: Tathāgatācintyaguhyanirdeśa Sūtra; Lamotte, Étienne, on Vajrapāṇi in the early Mahāyāna.
Getty, Alice, The Gods of Northern Buddhism (Clarendon Press, 1914), on Guhyakādhipati and the wrathful forms.

commentarial-tradition.body:
The ​Pāli ‌commentaries set ‌the ​first ​interpretive frame: ​identifying ​the ​Ambaṭṭha Sutta's ‌vajra-bearer ​with ​Sakka, ‌they read ​the ‌episode ​as the ‌deva-king's ​service ​to ​the dispensation ​— ​power ‌re-enlisted under ​wisdom.[^1]

‌The ​Sanskrit and ‌Tibetan ​traditions ‌built ​the esoteric ‌edifice ​on ​that base. ‌The ‌Guhyasamāja ‌commentarial ​lineages treat ​Vajrapāṇi ‌as ​the compiler ​and ‌guardian ​of the ​tantric ‌canon; ​the ‌Tibetan tradition ​makes ​Chana ​Dorjé one ​of ‌the ‌three great ​protectors ‌(rigs ​gsum ​mgon po) ‌whose ‌practice ‌is foundational ‌for ​initiates; ‌and ​the East ​Asian ​gate-guardian ‌cult — ​the ​Niō ​of Japan, ‌the ​Heng-Ha ​generals ​of China ‌— ​is ‌his commentarial ​tradition ‌in ​wood ‌and plaster: ‌an ​entire ​architecture of ​protection ​glossed ‌from one ‌bodhisattva's ​name.[^2]

sources.citation: Dīgha Nikāya 3 with its commentary (Sumaṅgalavilāsinī), on Vajirapāṇi as Sakka.
Getty, Alice, The Gods of Northern Buddhism (Clarendon Press, 1914).

original-script.body:
The ​name is ‌preserved ‌in ​Devanagari as ​**वज्रपाणि** ​— ​Brahmic abugida, ​attested ‌Vedic ​and Classical ​Sanskrit ‌(as ​Indra's epithet) ‌and ​Buddhist ‌Sanskrit (as ​the ​bodhisattva); the ​script ​is ​written left-to-right.[^1]

‌The ​scholarly ‌transliteration is ​*Vajrapāṇi* ‌(IAST), ​giving the ‌normalized ​reading ‌/ʋə.dʑrə.ˈpaː.ɳi/.

The ​rendering ​proceeds ‌step by ‌step:

‌- Sanskrit ​Vajrapāṇi ​is ‌written वज्रपाणि ​in ​Devanagari: ‌वज्र (vajra) ​+ ​पाणि ‌(pāṇi), ‘thunderbolt’ ​+ ‌‘hand’.
​- The ​compound ​is ​a bahuvrīhi: ‌‘in ‌whose ​hand is ‌the ​vajra’ — ​an ‌epithet ‌inherited from ‌the ‌Vedic ​Indra.
- ‌IAST ​encodes ​the long ​ā ‌with ​the macron ​and ​the ‌retroflex nasal ​with ​the underdotted ​ṇ.
‌- ​The Unicode ‌restoration ​Vajrapāṇi ‌is registrable ​in ‌.com; ‌the Devanagari ​form ​is ​not supported ​in ‌the ‌.com IDN ​table.[^2]

sources.citation: Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. vajrapāṇi.
Edgerton, Franklin, Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit Dictionary (Yale University Press, 1953), s.v. Vajrapāṇi.
